## Why this matters

Datasets outlive the people who create them. A clean, well-named, anonymized dataset can be reused, shared publicly and understood by the next student. A messy one becomes a liability. The code exercises on this page run in your browser: there is nothing to install. The first time, R takes a few seconds to load.

## Working with data [BA]{.ba-tag}

- Use Google Sheets whenever possible. Otherwise, prefer `.tsv` or `.csv` to `.xlsx`.
- Datasets are version controlled and stored in the cloud.
- Variable names are in **English** and are **both human and computer readable**: `hr_baseline`, not `HR baseline (bpm)!` or `v17`.
- Every dataset has a **unique ID variable**. Our participant IDs follow the lab format: "SE" plus 8 digits, for example `SE05685678` (see the [Participant ID template]({{< var links.tpl_participant_id >}})). No spaces, special or accented characters.
- Personal identifiers (email, Neptun code, etc.) are anonymized as soon as possible and **never used as IDs** in raw form.
- For questionnaires, document every item in a copy of the [scale keys template]({{< var links.tpl_scale_keys >}}): item code, wording, scale and subscale, whether it is reversed, and the response range. Scoring code reads this table, so reversed items and subscales can't be mixed up. An AI agent can prefill it from the questionnaire; check the reversed items yourself.

## Data analysis skills [BA]{.ba-tag}

Data analysis is a vast field, and there is always more to learn, so what I look for is the ability to learn new things. That said:

- You must know **(generalized) linear regression** fairly well. It is the foundation everything else builds on.
- Learn **linear mixed-effects models** (multilevel regression) as soon as possible.
- My data analysis and statistical inference lectures (in Hungarian) are in this [Google Classroom]({{< var links.classroom >}}). Use them whenever you need to.

## Tools [BA]{.ba-tag}

- I prefer open-source software. I don't work with SPSS. If you can't use R, use [JASP](https://jasp-stats.org/) or [jamovi](https://www.jamovi.org/).
- [Use R](https://www.r-project.org/). I encourage everyone who decides to learn it and can help with online courses. **If you are my PhD student, you must learn R.**
- Another language (MATLAB, Python, Julia) is fine, but I may not be able to help with your code.

## Programming in R

- I use R locally with [RStudio](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/).
- Use an **R Project** for every project. No standalone scripts.
- Use the [tidyverse](https://www.tidyverse.org/) and tidy tools whenever possible, because they are readable. Other packages I use often: `easystats` for residual diagnostics and publication-ready tables, and Quarto or `rmarkdown` for reports.
- Always use [git](https://git-scm.com/) and [GitHub](https://github.com/) for version control. It also makes collaboration, bug reporting and code review easy.
- Format code according to the [tidyverse style guide](https://style.tidyverse.org/).

## Analysis reports

- Analysis reports are written in Quarto (or R Markdown) and compiled to HTML.
- Include both explanatory text and code comments.
- The HTML can be hosted on GitHub Pages ([example]({{< var links.report_example >}})). Otherwise, use the [GitHub HTML preview](https://htmlpreview.github.io/) for HTML files in a repository.

## Practice in R

These exercises use the conventions above. Edit the code, press **Run Code**, then **Submit Answer** to get feedback.

### Exercise 1: Readable variable names [BA]{.ba-tag}

The pilot dataset `raw` came from a Hungarian survey export, with these column names:

| Current name | Contains | Rename to |
|---|---|---|
| `Résztvevő` | participant code | `participant` |
| `Életkor (év)` | age in years | `age_years` |
| `Pulzus nyugalomban!` | resting heart rate | `hr_baseline` |

Fill in the new names.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_names
library(dplyr)
raw <- data.frame(
  `Résztvevő` = c("P01", "P02", "P03"),
  `Életkor (év)` = c(21, 23, 22),
  `Pulzus nyugalomban!` = c(72, 80, 68),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_names
raw |>
  rename(
    ______ = `Résztvevő`,
    ______ = `Életkor (év)`,
    ______ = `Pulzus nyugalomban!`
  )
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_names
#| check: true
if (!is.data.frame(.result)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The result should be a data frame. Did the code run without errors?")
} else if (identical(names(.result), c("participant", "age_years", "hr_baseline"))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Nice: English, lowercase, no spaces or special characters.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = paste("Your column names are:", paste(names(.result), collapse = ", ")))
}
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_names" }
Inside `rename()`, the new name goes on the left and the old name, in backticks, goes on the right: `new_name = \`Old name\``.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_names" }
```r
raw |>
  rename(
    participant = `Résztvevő`,
    age_years = `Életkor (év)`,
    hr_baseline = `Pulzus nyugalomban!`
  )
```
:::

### Exercise 2: Proper ID variables [BA]{.ba-tag}

Lab IDs are built from three parts: "SE", the participant's birth **day** as two digits, the **last two digits** of their mother's birth year, and the **last four digits** of their phone number. A participant born on the 5th, whose mother was born in 1968 and whose phone number ends in 5678, gets `SE05685678`.

The `parts` data has these pieces in separate columns. Build the `id` column. Use `str_pad()` to pad the birth day to two digits, `str_sub()` to take the last two digits of the year, and `str_c()` to glue everything together.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_ids
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
parts <- data.frame(
  birth_day = c(5, 23, 9),
  mother_birth_year = c(1968, 1972, 2001),
  phone_last4 = c("5678", "0412", "9930")
)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_ids
parts |>
  mutate(id = str_c(
    "SE",
    str_pad(birth_day, width = ______, pad = ______),
    str_sub(mother_birth_year, start = ______),
    phone_last4
  ))
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_ids
#| check: true
target <- c("SE05685678", "SE23720412", "SE09019930")
if (!is.data.frame(.result) || !"id" %in% names(.result)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The result should be a data frame with an `id` column.")
} else if (identical(as.character(.result$id), target)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. Every ID has the same length and matches the lab format (^SE\\d{8}$).")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = paste("Your IDs:", paste(.result$id, collapse = ", "), "- expected", paste(target, collapse = ", ")))
}
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_ids" }
For the birth day, `width = 2` and `pad = "0"` turn `5` into `"05"`. For the year, a negative `start` counts from the end: `str_sub(1968, start = -2)` gives `"68"`.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_ids" }
```r
parts |>
  mutate(id = str_c(
    "SE",
    str_pad(birth_day, width = 2, pad = "0"),
    str_sub(mother_birth_year, start = -2),
    phone_last4
  ))
```
:::

### Exercise 3: Remove personal identifiers [BA]{.ba-tag}

The dataset `survey` already has a proper `id`, but it still contains participants' `email` and `neptun` columns. Create an anonymized version without them.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_anon
library(dplyr)
survey <- data.frame(
  id = c("SE05685678", "SE23720412", "SE09019930"),
  email = c("a@example.com", "b@example.com", "c@example.com"),
  neptun = c("ABC123", "DEF456", "GHI789"),
  stress = c(3, 5, 2)
)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_anon
survey |>
  select(______)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_anon
#| check: true
if (!is.data.frame(.result)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The result should be a data frame.")
} else if (any(c("email", "neptun") %in% names(.result))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Personal identifiers are still in the data.")
} else if (!all(c("id", "stress") %in% names(.result))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "You removed too much: keep `id` and `stress`.")
} else {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. Only this anonymized version may ever be shared or published.")
}
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_anon" }
In `select()`, a minus sign drops a column: `select(-column_name)`.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_anon" }
```r
survey |>
  select(-email, -neptun)
```
:::

### Exercise 4: A first regression

Fit a linear regression predicting `stress` from `caffeine_mg` in the `study` data, and return the slope (the coefficient of `caffeine_mg`).

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_lm
set.seed(42)
study <- data.frame(caffeine_mg = round(runif(40, 0, 300)))
study$stress <- round(2 + 0.01 * study$caffeine_mg + rnorm(40, 0, 0.8), 1)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_lm
fit <- lm(______ ~ ______, data = study)
coef(fit)[______]
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_lm
#| check: true
target <- unname(coef(lm(stress ~ caffeine_mg, data = study))["caffeine_mg"])
if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1 && isTRUE(all.equal(unname(.result), target))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = sprintf("Correct: stress increases by about %.3f points per mg of caffeine. Per 100 mg, that's %.2f points.", target, 100 * target))
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not yet. The outcome goes on the left of `~`, and you want the single coefficient named \"caffeine_mg\".")
}
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_lm" }
The formula is `outcome ~ predictor`. Coefficients can be selected by name: `coef(fit)["caffeine_mg"]`.
:::

::: { .solution exercise="ex_lm" }
```r
fit <- lm(stress ~ caffeine_mg, data = study)
coef(fit)["caffeine_mg"]
```
:::

## Check yourself

::: quiz
Which of these is a good ID for a participant?

- [ ] `kovács.anna@gmail.com`
- [ ] `ÁB 7`
- [x] `SE05685678`
- [ ] `7`

::: explain
Lab IDs are "SE" plus 8 digits, with no spaces, special or accented characters. They are never raw personal identifiers such as names or email addresses.
:::
:::

::: quiz
Which variable name follows the lab's conventions?

- [ ] `Szívfrekvencia nyugalomban`
- [ ] `HR (bpm) - baseline!`
- [x] `hr_baseline`
- [ ] `var17`

::: explain
English, human-readable and computer-readable: lowercase, no spaces or special characters, and descriptive.
:::
:::

::: quiz
You need a quick analysis for your project. Which setup fits the lab's workflow?

- [ ] An SPSS syntax file on your laptop.
- [ ] A standalone `analysis.R` script emailed to the supervisor.
- [x] An R Project under git, with a Quarto report pushed to GitHub.

::: explain
Every project gets an R Project, code is version controlled with git and GitHub, and reports are written in Quarto and compiled to HTML.
